problem: It calls 0.6991 dB/km 'a fair value for good single-mode fiber at 1550 nm'. Standard single-mode fiber at 1550 nm loses about 0.19–0.22 dB/km. 0.70 dB/km is three times too high for good fiber at that window, so the sentence teaches a wrong benchmark.
fix: Replace with: 'This is much higher than the ~0.2 dB/km of modern single-mode fiber at 1550 nm, more like old or poor-quality fiber, but the arithmetic is what the question asks. An OTDR on the same fiber must show the same slope, 0.6991 dB/km.'

where: Worked example 2 (and quiz Q5), opening line
problem: It says 'The same fiber on an OTDR: group delay reads 500.0 ps at 1548 nm…'. An OTDR measures backscatter loss against distance; it does not measure group delay against wavelength, so it cannot give dispersion. The instrument named belongs to another method.
fix: Say: 'The same fiber in a pulse-delay (time-of-flight) dispersion set-up: the relative group delay reads 500.0 ps at 1548 nm and 506.8 ps at 1552 nm over 10 km.'

problem: 500.0 ps is presented as the group delay through 10 km of fiber. The true delay is about L·n_g/c ≈ 10⁴ m × 1.47 ÷ (3 × 10⁸ m/s) ≈ 49 μs, a hundred thousand times larger. Only a delay difference can be a few hundred picoseconds.
fix: Call the numbers relative (differential) group delays measured against a reference wavelength, and keep the difference dτ = 6.8 ps as the only quantity used: 'relative group delay 500.0 ps at 1548 nm and 506.8 ps at 1552 nm, so dτ = 6.8 ps over dλ = 4 nm'.

where: Worked example 2 answer, and quiz Q5
problem: D = 0.17 ps/(nm·km) at 1550 nm is the value for dispersion-shifted fiber, not the standard single-mode fiber implied by Worked example 1, which would give about 17 ps/(nm·km). Calling it 'the same fiber' confuses two different fiber types.
fix: Add one line: 'This near-zero D at 1550 nm means the sample is dispersion-shifted fiber; ordinary single-mode fiber would show about 17 ps/(nm·km) here.' (Or change dτ to 68 ps so D = 1.7, still not 17 — better to label the fiber type.)

where: Section 2, first reading of the trace
problem: 'The slope of the straight part is α in dB/km' hides the round trip. Rayleigh backscatter travels out and back, so the raw trace falls at 2α per km; only after the instrument halves it does the slope equal the one-way α. A student may then treat a raw dB difference between markers as one-way loss (as in quiz Q4).
fix: Write: 'The trace falls at 2α per kilometre because the light travels out and back; the OTDR halves this, so the α it reports, and the slope of the display, is the one-way value in dB/km. Quiz readings are taken from that corrected display.'

problem: 'A value like 17 ps/nm for a whole spool is not the coefficient' is muddled: for a 1 km spool the total 17 ps/nm and the coefficient 17 ps/(nm·km) have the same number, so the example does not show the confusion it means to show.
fix: Use a different length: '40 ps/nm measured on a 10 km spool is a total, not a coefficient; divide by 10 km to get 4 ps/(nm·km).'
